newsitem.title: NEW ZEALAND: NZ dlr itching to go lower but held back -analysts.
newsitem.headline: NZ dlr itching to go lower but held back -analysts.

text.p: Recent volatility in the New Zealand dollar shows no sign of abating in the short term, analysts said on Friday.

Technical analysts said the kiwi was in a strong downward trend, but foreign exchange dealers said they were reluctant to take it too low without an off-setting rise in interest rates, after the Reserve Bank of New Zealand (RBNZ) rapped markets over the knuckles on Thursday for easing conditions too far.
"The market is clearly going to be disappointed if they think the RB is going to allow them to keep easing conditions," said Bankers Trust New Zealand dealer Phil Lindberg.
"It's clearly too early to think they'll allow the market to take it where it wants."
However, a senior Wellington foreign exchange dealer said he expected short rates, currently at 7.17 percent, to rise towards eight percent "in the short term".
That would take pressure off conditions and open the door for a further fall in the currency's Trade Weighted Index (TWI).
The kiwi's inclination to trend lower was clearly demonstrated by its reaction to Thursday's RBNZ warning.
Short rates bore the brunt of the statement by rising around 20 basis points, while the kiwi edged up only temporarily before selling down again.
The TWI has now stabilised at around 66.30 from 66.52 at Thursday's open.
Conditions have tightened to 60 basis points (in interest rate terms) below the RBNZ's desired levels, from 75 b.p. shortly before the RBNZ spoke out on Thursday.
A week ago the bank said it would tolerate a variation of 50 b.p. either side of its assumptions.
Bankers Trust deputy chief executive John Macfarlane said while overall conditions might not have tightened to the degree the RBNZ hoped, it should take comfort from the prevailing mix.
"Yes, conditions are falling, but interest rates are rising and the currency is falling which is what they have been wanting for some time," he said.
Macfarlane said a lower currency would help the tradeable sector, and higher interest rates would dampen the housing market, the source of much of the inflationary pressure seen in the last year.
Bank of New Zealand technical analyst Keith Black said US$0.6780/90 capped the kiwi at the moment, with the immediate risk that it would attempt to break below US$0.6730/40.
The kiwi traded at 0.6776/83 at 0400 GMT on Friday.
ANZ bank technical analyst Mark Elliott said that by breaking below 68 U.S. cents for the first time in a year, the kiwi had moved to a new lower range.
"Over the next several weeks or maybe the next couple of months I would see a move to at least the high 0.66s, low 0.67s, and quite possibly down to the mid 0.6400 area," Elliott said.

A Wellington dealer said settlement of recent eurokiwi issues should help buoy the kiwi, and another said much of the supply in the currency on Thursday had now been cleared and he saw the kiwi tracking slowly higher over the next few weeks.
Lindberg said while the currency seemed to be in an overall downtrend, it remained highly sensitive on a TWI basis to movements in the Australian dollar and the yen.
